solution:
a. Crystallisation.

Section 3.2.1 gives crystallisation as the method for exactly this material: "When a crude solid is made of mainly one substance and has some impurities, it is purified by the process of crystallization." It is carried out in four steps — preparation of a saturated solution of the crude solid in a hot solvent, hot filtration to take out the undissolved impurities as residue, cooling of the filtrate so that the main solute (whose solubility falls as the temperature falls) comes out as crystals while the small amount of soluble impurity stays behind in the mother liquor, and filtration to collect the crystals. The crystals so obtained are free from both soluble and insoluble impurities.

Distillation is not the method here. Section 3.3 defines it as a way to separate volatile liquids from non-volatile impurities, or two liquids whose boiling points differ sufficiently — it works on liquids, not on the purification of a solid organic compound.

Both terms come from filtration, in which a solution is poured on to a moist filter-paper cone fitted in a funnel with a beaker kept below it (section 3.2).

a. Residue — the insoluble part that is left behind on the filter paper.

b. Filtrate — the liquid that passes through the filter paper and is collected in the beaker below.

In crystallisation the same two words are used twice over: during hot filtration the undissolved impurities are the residue, and at the last step the filtrate left after the pure crystals have been filtered off is given its own name, the mother liquor.

A condenser is used to turn the vapour back into a liquid so that the purified substance can be collected.

Distillation works in two stages (section 3.3.1): the liquid is first converted into its vapour by boiling, and then "the vapour is condensed back into liquid by cooling and the pure liquid trickles down in the reciver." The condenser is what performs the second stage. It is a tube surrounded by a jacket through which cold water is circulated, so the vapours that leave the side arm of the round-bottom flask meet a cool surface, give up their heat, condense, and run down into the receiver.

Without a condenser the vapour would simply escape into the air and the distillate — the pure liquid the whole operation is being done to obtain — would be lost.

The chapter states that the paper is moistened, in both forms of filtration it describes, but it does not state the reason.

What the chapter does say: in simple filtration a circular piece of filter paper is folded into a cone and fitted in the funnel, and "The paper is made moist, the solution to be filtered is poured on the filter paper" (section 3.2). In filtration under suction a circular filter paper of the correct size is laid on the porous bottom of the Buchner funnel and "It is moistened with a few drops of water or solvent" before the pump is started; Fig. 3.2 labels that part of the assembly "moistened filter paper".

[Not stated in this chapter — standard laboratory practice.] Wetting makes the paper cling to the glass of the funnel or to the porous plate. It therefore stays seated and does not lift, curl or shift when the liquid is poured on it or when suction is applied, and no gap is left between the paper and the funnel through which unfiltered liquid could run past the edge of the paper and carry the solid into the filtrate.

The stationary phase is water — specifically the water trapped in the fibres of the chromatography paper.

Section 3.5.2 describes paper chromatography as an example of partition chromatography, in which both phases are liquids. A special quality paper, Whatmann paper number 1, is used, and "The water trapped in the fibres of the paper acts as the stationary phase." The paper itself is only the support that holds this water; it is not the stationary phase.

The mobile phase is the solvent in the chamber, which rises up the paper by capillary action and flows over the spot, and separation occurs because the components partition themselves differently between the two liquid phases.

The condenser would cool the vapours poorly, so condensation would be incomplete and part of the distillate would be lost as vapour at the receiver end.

The chapter shows the correct connection in Fig. 3.4: the condenser jacket has two openings, the "water inlet" at the lower end and the "water outlet" at the upper end, and section 3.3.1 says the condenser "is kept cool by circulating water through its jacket". So the cooling water is meant to be fed in at the bottom and to leave at the top.

[The chapter shows this arrangement but does not state what goes wrong if it is reversed; the following follows from it.] If the tap is connected to the upper outlet instead, the water enters at the top and drains out of the bottom under gravity faster than it is supplied. The jacket never stays completely full, air pockets remain against the inner tube, and much less of the condenser surface is actually in contact with cold water. Cooling is therefore inefficient and the flow is unsteady. Two further consequences: the vapour is no longer met by the coldest water at the far end of its path, and the sudden, uneven contact of cold water with hot glass risks cracking the condenser.

Alumina and silica gel.

Section 3.5.1 names both for adsorption chromatography: in column chromatography "The stationary phase material can be Alumina, Silica gel", a slurry of which is packed into a long glass tube; and in thin layer chromatography a thin layer about 0.2 mm thick "of adsorbent silica gel or alumina spread over a glass plate acts as the stationary phase".

(The chapter gives a third material of a different kind: in paper chromatography the stationary phase is the water held in the fibres of Whatmann paper number 1.)

From section 3.4, the organic solvent used for solvent extraction must have these properties.

1. The substance to be extracted must be more soluble in it than in the aqueous solution — extraction takes place "based on the difference in solubility of compound in two liquids", and it is this difference that drives the solute out of the aqueous phase into the organic phase.

2. It must be immiscible with water, so that on shaking the two liquids do not mix but settle into two separate layers which can be run off from one another; the chapter states that "The organic liquid should be immiscible with water and be able to form two layers."

3. It should be readily removable by distillation, since the chapter's own procedure ends with "The organic solvent is, then, removed by distillation and the solute is collected" — that is, the solvent must be volatile enough to be distilled off, leaving the extracted solute behind.

Because the spot must be carried up the stationary phase by the mobile phase, not dissolved away into it.

The chapter states the requirement twice. For thin layer chromatography (section 3.5.1) the plate is "placed in a closed jar containing the mobile phase such that the spot is well above the mobile phase", and for paper chromatography (section 3.5.2) the paper is suspended in the chamber "taking care that the spot does not dip in the mobile phase".

[The chapter states the requirement rather than the consequence; the following follows from it.] If the spot were below the level of the solvent it would sit immersed in the pool of mobile phase. The mixture would simply dissolve off the plate or paper into that pool instead of being picked up by the solvent front as it rises. The components would never travel different distances over the stationary phase, so no separated spots and no chromatogram would be obtained, and no retention factor could be measured, since \(R_f\) is defined from the distance the solute travels from the base line.

a. Stationary phase — one of the two phases used in chromatography (section 3.5). It is the phase that stays fixed in place, over which the mobile phase is allowed to move; the components of the mixture are held on it to different extents and so travel at different rates and get separated. It can be a solid or a liquid, and it is the nature of the stationary phase that divides chromatography into adsorption chromatography (solid, for example alumina or silica gel) and partition chromatography (liquid, for example the water held in the fibres of chromatography paper).

b. Saturated solution — section 3.2.1 defines it as a solution which cannot dissolve any additional quantity of solute. In crystallisation such a solution is prepared by boiling the crude solid in a small but sufficient quantity of a suitable solvent; the solution is then almost saturated with respect to the main solute, but not with respect to the soluble impurities, because those are present in only a small proportion.

Both convert a liquid to vapour and condense it back, but they differ in when they can be used and in the apparatus (sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2).

| | Simple distillation | Fractional distillation |
|---|---|---|
| When it is used | The components differ sufficiently in boiling point, or a volatile liquid is to be freed from a non-volatile impurity | The difference in the boiling points of the two liquids is not appreciable, so simple distillation cannot separate them |
| Apparatus | Round bottom flask with a thermometer, side arm, condenser and receiver | The same assembly, but with a fractionating column fitted between the distillation flask and the condenser |
| Path of the vapour | The vapour passes straight from the side arm into the condenser | The vapour first passes through the fractionating column and only then reaches the condenser |
| What happens inside | One vaporisation followed by one condensation | Repeated exchange between the ascending vapours and the descending liquid; the vapours of the less volatile liquid are scrubbed off by the descending liquid, so the rising vapour becomes richer and richer in the more volatile component |
| Example from the chapter | Acetone (b.p. \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) and water (b.p. \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) | Acetone (b.p. 329 K) and methyl alcohol (b.p. 337.7 K); acetone and benzene (353 K) |

a. Solvent extraction — section 3.4. When an organic substance is present in an aqueous solution it can be extracted from that solution by shaking it with an organic solvent in which the substance is more soluble. The organic liquid must be immiscible with water and form two layers; the solute distributes itself between the two immiscible liquids and passes from the aqueous phase into the organic phase. On shaking a few times with small volumes of the organic phase most of the solute is extracted, and the organic solvent is then removed by distillation and the solute collected.

b. Distillation — section 3.3. It is the method in which a liquid is converted into its vapour by boiling and the vapour is then condensed back into a liquid by cooling and collected in a receiver. It is used to separate (i) volatile liquids from non-volatile impurities and (ii) liquids having a sufficient difference in their boiling points.

Section 3.2.1, under "Choice of the solvent", lists three properties a solvent must have for crystallisation.

1. The compound to be crystallised should be least or sparingly soluble in the solvent at room temperature but highly soluble at high temperature. This is what makes the method work: nearly all of the compound dissolves in the hot solvent and comes back out as crystals when the solution cools.

2. The solvent should not react chemically with the compound to be purified, otherwise the compound would be altered instead of purified.

3. The solvent should be volatile, so that it can be removed easily from the crystals.

The solvents generally used are water, ethyl alcohol, methyl alcohol, acetone, ether or their combinations, and the chapter notes that the choice among them is made by trial and error.

Chromatography separates the components of a mixture by distributing them between a stationary phase and a mobile phase, and depending on what the stationary phase is, section 3.5 classifies it into two types.

1. Adsorption chromatography (section 3.5.1). Principle — differential adsorption: different solutes are adsorbed on the solid stationary phase to different extents, so as the mobile phase carries them along, the more strongly adsorbed component is held back and the less strongly adsorbed one moves ahead, and they separate. It is of two kinds:
(i) Column chromatography, in which a slurry of the adsorbent (alumina or silica gel) is packed in a long glass tube, the mixture is loaded on top and the mobile phase is poured over it; the components separate into bands down the column, the least strongly adsorbed being desorbed and eluted first.
(ii) Thin layer chromatography, in which a thin layer about 0.2 mm thick of silica gel or alumina spread on a glass plate is the stationary phase; the mixture is applied as a small spot about 2 cm from one end and the plate is stood in a closed jar containing the mobile phase, which rises and carries the components up to different distances.

2. Partition chromatography (section 3.5.2). Principle — continuous differential partitioning: here both the stationary and the mobile phase are liquids, and the components are separated because each one partitions itself between the two liquid phases to a different degree. Paper chromatography is the example given: the water trapped in the fibres of Whatmann paper number 1 is the stationary phase, the solvent rising by capillary action is the mobile phase, and the developed paper strip is the chromatogram.

Because the components of the mixture are adsorbed on the stationary phase to different extents and therefore travel down the column at different rates.

Section 3.5.1 explains it for column chromatography. The mixture is loaded on top of the adsorbent column and moves down with the mobile phase; "The solutes get adsorbed on the stationary phase and depending on the degree to which they are adsorbed, the solutes get separated from each other. The most strongly adsorbed component is retained on the column and others move down the column to various distances forming bands."

So a component that is held only weakly by the adsorbent is desorbed easily and keeps moving with the solvent, while one that is held strongly spends more of its time on the adsorbent and lags behind. After some time each component occupies its own zone at its own depth in the column, and these zones are the bands we see. The weakly adsorbed component is desorbed first and leaves the column first, and the strongly adsorbed one is eluted later, so the bands emerge one after another and the solutions can be collected separately.

Coloured components are seen directly as coloured spots. A colourless component leaves no visible spot, so it has to be made visible, and the chapter gives three ways of doing it (sections 3.5.1 and 3.5.2).

1. Under UV light. If the component is not coloured but has the property of fluorescence, the plate or paper is examined under ultraviolet light, where the spot glows and can be marked.

2. In an iodine chamber. The plate is kept in a chamber containing a few iodine crystals; the iodine vapours are adsorbed by the components and the spots appear brown.

3. With a spraying agent. A reagent is sprayed over the plate which reacts with the component to give a coloured spot — the chapter's example is amino acids, which are visualised by spraying the plate with a solution of ninhydrin.

Section 3.5.2 sums it up for both techniques: the coloured components are visible as coloured spots, and the colourless components are observed under UV light or by using a spraying agent.

Both are chromatographic techniques carried out on a flat surface, and both begin by applying the mixture as a small spot about 2 cm from one end and end with a developed chromatogram from which \(R_f\) values can be measured. They differ in the phases involved (sections 3.5.1 and 3.5.2).

| | Thin layer chromatography (TLC) | Paper chromatography |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Adsorption chromatography | Partition chromatography |
| Stationary phase | A thin layer, about 0.2 mm thick, of adsorbent silica gel or alumina | The water trapped in the fibres of the paper |
| Support | A glass plate — the plate is called the TLC plate or chromplate | A special quality paper, Whatmann paper number 1 |
| State of the two phases | Stationary phase solid, mobile phase liquid | Both phases liquid |
| Principle | Differential adsorption — the components are adsorbed on the stationary phase to different extents | Continuous differential partitioning of the components between the two liquid phases |
| How the plate or paper is set up | Placed in a closed jar containing the mobile phase so that the spot is well above the mobile phase | Suspended in a chamber containing the mobile phase, taking care that the spot does not dip into it |
| Movement of the mobile phase | Rises up the plate, carrying the components different distances according to their degree of adsorption | Rises up the paper by capillary action and flows over the spot |

Detection is the same for both: coloured components appear as coloured spots, and colourless ones are observed under UV light, in an iodine chamber, or by using a spraying agent such as ninhydrin.

The diagram is the assembly for **filtration under suction**, the same set-up as Fig. 3.2 of this chapter.

**Labels, from the top down**
1. Büchner funnel — the porcelain funnel with the wide cylindrical body standing on top of the flask.
2. Moistened filter paper — the circular filter paper of the correct size, shown as the broken line lying across the flat bottom of the funnel.
3. Porous plate — the perforated circular bottom of the Büchner funnel on which that filter paper rests.
4. Rubber bung (rubber cork) — the collar that seats the stem of the funnel in the mouth of the flask and makes the joint airtight.
5. Büchner flask — the thick-walled conical flask below the funnel, carrying a side arm.
6. Side arm and rubber tubing — the tube leading off the neck of the flask, through which the flask is connected to a safety bottle and beyond it to the suction (vacuum) pump.
7. Filtrate — the liquid collected at the bottom of the flask after passing through the filter paper.

**The process**

Filtration carried out with the help of a vacuum pump is called filtration under suction, and it is faster and more efficient than simple filtration.

The circular filter paper is laid on the porous bottom of the Büchner funnel and moistened with a few drops of water or solvent, and the funnel is fitted into the thick-walled conical flask with the rubber cork. The side arm of the flask is joined by rubber tubing to a safety bottle, which is in turn connected to the pump; the safety bottle is there to prevent the filtrate being sucked over into the suction pump.

The mixture to be filtered is poured into the funnel and the pump is started. This lowers the pressure inside the flask, so the liquid is drawn through the filter paper much more quickly than it would drain under gravity alone. The solid particles are too large to pass through the pores of the paper and stay behind on it as the residue — in a crystallisation this is where the pure crystals are collected — while the liquid passes through and collects in the flask as the filtrate.

A thick-walled flask is used because the flask is under reduced pressure from the outside while the pump is running.
